title: Chapter LIX

teacherSummary.text: Elizabeth tells Jane, who is astonished; Elizabeth jokes she began to love Darcy on seeing Pemberley's grounds. Darcy asks Mr. Bennet's consent; Mr. Bennet questions Elizabeth seriously, fearing she might marry without respect. She explains Darcy's goodness and his role in Lydia's marriage. Mrs. Bennet is dazzled by his wealth.

vocabulary.context: Darcy was not of a disposition in which happiness overflows in mirth; and Elizabeth, agitated and confused, rather knew that she was happy, than felt herself to be so; for, besides the immediate embarrassment, there were other evils before her.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “overflow”: over- (Old English ofer, "over"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: An adjective expressing some quality, attribute, or relation, that is properly or specially appropriate to a person…
vocabulary.context: Elizabeth could hardly help laughing at so convenient a proposal; yet was really vexed that her mother should be always giving him such an epithet.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “epithet”: the (Greek theos, "god"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary.

vocabulary.context: She could not determine how her mother would take it; sometimes doubting whether all his wealth and grandeur would be enough to overcome her abhorrence of the man.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “doubting”: -ing (Old English -ing, action). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.context: It will save me a world of trouble and economy.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “economy”: no root in our classroom table; have students look it up (Etymonline, OED) and record the language of origin.

vocabulary.context: If this be the case, he deserves you.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “deserve”: de- (Latin de, "down from, away"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.context: Were it for nothing but his love of you, I must always have esteemed him; but now, as Bingley’s friend and your husband, there can be only Bingley and yourself more dear to me.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “esteem”: no root in our classroom table; have students look it up (Etymonline, OED) and record the language of origin.

vocabulary.definition: That emotion which is excited by novelty, or the presentation to the sight or mind of something new, unusual,…
vocabulary.context: “This is an evening of wonders, indeed!
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “wonder”: -er (Old English -ere, "one who"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: To fear in a great degree
vocabulary.context: Everything was too recent for gaiety, but the evening passed tranquilly away; there was no longer anything material to be dreaded, and the comfort of ease and familiarity would come in time.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “dread”: no root in our classroom table; have students look it up (Etymonline, OED) and record the language of origin.

vocabulary.definition: The act of applying or laying on, in a literal sense
vocabulary.context: Elizabeth reserved to herself the application for her mother’s.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “application”: ap- (Latin ad, "to") + plic (Latin plicare, "to fold") + -ation (Latin -atio, "the act or result of"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary.

vocabulary.context: Elizabeth told her the motives of her secrecy.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “motive”: mot (Latin movere, "to move") + -ive (Latin -ivus, "tending to"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary.

context.history: A father's consent was legally and socially central.

significance: Mr. Bennet finally acts like a caring father.
discussionQuestions: Why does Mr. Bennet worry about Elizabeth?
Where does characterization appear in this chapter, and what effect does it have? Point to one passage.
How does this chapter connect to the book's larger concern with class and social mobility?

writingPrompts.label: Middle School
writingPrompts.text: In “Chapter LIX,” how does Austen show confiding and consent? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the chapter, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the characterization you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: HS Freshman
writingPrompts.text: In Chapter LIX, how does Austen develop the idea of confiding and consent? State a clear claim, support it with two or three quotations, and explain how the characterization in the chapter helps build that idea.

writingPrompts.label: HS Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how Chapter LIX develops the idea of confiding and consent. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of characterization and plot shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.

writingPrompts.label: HS Junior
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how the structure of Chapter LIX (where it begins, turns and ends) and its characterization shape the reader's understanding of confiding and consent. Identify one place where the text leaves matters uncertain and explain how that uncertainty adds to its meaning.

writingPrompts.label: HS Senior
writingPrompts.text: Two readers disagree about what Chapter LIX suggests about confiding and consent. Lay out two plausible interpretations, weigh the evidence for each (including the chapter's characterization and plot), and argue for the stronger one in a sustained, well-organized essay.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how Jane Austen uses characterization in Chapter LIX to complicate the reader's understanding of confiding and consent. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate Chapter LIX within its historical and literary context and argue how the chapter's treatment of confiding and consent responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: College Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Read Chapter LIX alongside the conventions of its genre and period. Argue how the chapter's handling of confiding and consent follows or bends those conventions, using the characterization as evidence, and test your reading against one published critic. Document two secondary sources in MLA.

writingPrompts.label: College Junior
writingPrompts.text: Apply a named critical approach (for example formalist, historicist, feminist, psychoanalytic or ecocritical) to Chapter LIX and its treatment of confiding and consent. State your method, show what it reveals in the chapter's characterization and plot, and identify where the text resists it.

writingPrompts.label: College Senior
writingPrompts.text: Develop a research argument that reads Chapter LIX as evidence for a larger claim about confiding and consent in Pride and Prejudice. Connect close reading of the chapter to the whole novel, engage at least four scholarly sources, and state precisely where your reading departs from theirs (Chicago style).

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads Chapter LIX as a hinge in the novel's larger treatment of confiding and consent. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on Pride and Prejudice.

satQuestions.passage: The evening passed quietly, unmarked by anything extraordinary. The acknowledged lovers talked and laughed, the unacknowledged were silent. Darcy was not of a disposition in which happiness overflows in mirth; and Elizabeth, agitated and confused, rather knew that she was happy, than felt herself to be so; for, besides the immediate embarrassment, there were other evils before her. She anticipated what would be felt in the family when her situation became known; she was aware that no one liked him but Jane; and even feared that with the others it was a dislike which not all his fortune and consequence might do away.
satQuestions.prompt: Which choice best states a central concern of “Chapter LIX”?

segments.activity: Respond in writing to the bell-ringer, then pair-share.
segments.script: Settle in and write for five minutes: Why does Mr. Bennet worry about Elizabeth? No wrong answers yet; we will test these ideas against the text. Two volunteers share, and I note key words on the board.

segments.activity: Introduce 5 key words: pronounce, define from context, then the word's history.
segments.script: Today's words are overflows, epithet, doubting, economy, deserves. For each one we read the sentence, guess from context and then check Webster's. Here is the first: “Darcy was not of a disposition in which happiness overflows in mirth; and Elizabeth, agitated and confused, rather knew that she was happy, than felt herself to be so; for, besides the immediate embarrassment, there were other evils before her.” Webster's says: To flow over. Now the word history: “overflow”: over- (Old English ofer, "over"). Root not in our table: have students find it. “epithet”: the (Greek theos, "god"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary. “doubting”: -ing (Old English -ing, action). Root not in our table: have students find it. Add each root to your etymology log.

segments.activity: Present the historical and literary background.
segments.script: Here is what the first readers of Pride and Prejudice would have known. A father's consent was legally and socially central. Why does this chapter matter? Mr. Bennet finally acts like a caring father. Write down one question you want answered.

segments.activity: Teacher models a think-aloud on the anchor passage for characterization.
segments.script: Watch me read this the way a careful reader does. I read a sentence, stop, and ask what the author is doing. When I see characterization, I underline it and write in the margin what effect it has. Here I notice the diction and the sentence rhythm, and I connect them to confiding and consent.

segments.activity: Read the anchor passage aloud together; annotate for Characterization, Plot, Irony.
segments.script: Now we do it together. I read the first sentence and you track along. Mark every example of characterization. Turn to a partner: what does the author want us to notice? I will collect three ideas and we choose the strongest using evidence.
segments.passage: The evening passed quietly, unmarked by anything extraordinary. The acknowledged lovers talked and laughed, the unacknowledged were silent. Darcy was not of a disposition in which happiness overflows in mirth; and Elizabeth, agitated and confused, rather knew that she was happy, than felt herself to be so; for, besides the immediate embarrassment, there were other evils before her. She anticipated what would be felt in the family when her situation became known; she was aware that no one liked him but Jane; and even feared that with the others it was a dislike which not all his fortune and consequence might do away.

segments.activity: Students annotate a new passage independently in the reader, then begin the writing prompt at their rigor.
segments.script: Your turn. Annotate the next page in the app for Characterization, Plot, Irony: at least three marks with a margin note each. Then open your writing prompt; your level is already set. Middle-school version: In “Chapter LIX,” how does Austen show confiding and consent? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the chapter, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the characterization you noticed as one piece of evidence. I will circulate and conference.

segments.activity: Structured discussion (think-pair-share or a short Socratic circle).
segments.script: Let's talk. Our question: How does this chapter connect to first impressions and prejudice? Every claim needs a page reference. Respond to the person before you by agreeing, extending or challenging with evidence.

segments.activity: Chapter quiz in the app, then a one-sentence exit ticket.
segments.script: Take the chapter quiz in the app. Then, in one sentence, tell me what this chapter suggests about confiding and consent, backed by one short quotation.

segments.activity: Summarize the lesson and preview the next reading.
segments.script: Today we saw how characterization shapes confiding and consent. Tonight, read the next chapter and add two words to your etymology log.
